tests_notes: Empty and constant input, a hand-checked case, mean and spread properties, precision at a 1e9 offset; workload: 80000 sensor readings.

A.strategy: Variance from sums, no deviations list
A.rationale: The variance equals the mean of squares minus the squared mean, and math.sumprod gives the sum of squares in C. That drops the stored deviations list and a full Python-level pass.

B.rationale: Delegate the mean and the population standard deviation to the standard library, which computes them accurately, and keep only the scaling pass in Python.

C.strategy: map with the bound float multiply
C.rationale: Conservative micro-optimization: map calls scale.__mul__ from C for every deviation, replacing the per-item bytecode of the final list comprehension.

A.diagnosis: test_large_offset_keeps_precision failed: near 1e9 the mean of squares and the squared mean agree to every bit, so their difference cancels and the variance is lost.
A.rationale: Keeps the stable two-pass method: deviations from the mean first, then the spread as their Euclidean norm over sqrt(n), computed by math.hypot in one C call.

B.diagnosis: Rejected as too slow: statistics.pstdev sums squares with exact fractions and ran over seven times slower than the original. Compute the spread in floating point.
B.rationale: Keeps statistics.fmean for an accurately rounded mean and computes the variance from the deviations with math.sumprod in C, as the original does, instead of exact fractions.

notes: An honest no-win story. The one-pass variance is numerically unsafe and a test catches it; the safe repair is within noise. statistics.pstdev is exact but over 4x slower, so the differential check rejects it as a timeout; its repair and the bound-method map are slower.
